questions.title: Does 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3) impose a mandatory duty on the Office of Special Counsel to investigate alleged arbitrary FOIA withholdings?
questions.question_body: In *America First Legal Foundation v. Jamieson Greer* the D.C. Circuit discusses whether OSC must investigate an alleged FOIA violation under § 1216(a)(3) even when the triggers in FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) are not met. I’m confused about how these statutes interact. Does § 1216 create an absolute obligation for OSC to launch an investigation, or is it still discretionary? And if it is mandatory, why did the district court find that OSC’s refusal was only an error of law rather than a deprivation of a statutory right?

questions.title: How do courts apply the ‘relaxed’ standing test for procedural‑injury claims under Article III?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites *Center for Law & Education v. Dep’t of Educ.* and says that plaintiffs alleging violation of a procedural right get ‘relaxed’ standing requirements, but they still must show injury in fact and causation. What exactly changes under this relaxed standard? Which elements are still required, and how have courts interpreted "concrete interest" and "redressability" in similar procedural‑injury cases?

questions.title: Why can’t AFL claim Article III standing based on its failure to receive FOIA records from DOJ because OSC refused to investigate?
questions.question_body: *America First Legal* argues that AFL’s informational injury from DOJ’s non‑production is too attenuated from OSC’s decision not to investigate. I’m trying to understand how courts evaluate causation and redressability across multiple agencies. What level of speculation is permissible before a causal chain is considered too remote? Are there precedents that explain why an agency’s refusal to enforce its own statutory duties cannot give rise to standing against another agency’s unrelated action?

questions.title: What is ‘informational standing’ and does a statutory entitlement automatically confer it?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses ‘informational injury’ and references cases like *Zivotofsky v. Sec’y of State* and *AFC v. Feld*. If a statute (e.g., § 552 or § 1216) grants a party a right to receive certain information, does that automatically give rise to Article III standing when that information is withheld? Or must there be an additional concrete injury beyond the mere denial of the statutory right?

questions.title: What does ‘de novo’ review mean when an appellate court vacates a district court judgment on jurisdictional grounds?
questions.question_body: *America First Legal* notes that its review is de novo after the district court dismissed the case for failure to state a claim but also addressed standing later. I’m unclear on what de novo review entails here: Does it mean the appellate panel re‑examines every factual and legal issue afresh, or is its scope limited because the dismissal was based on subject‑matter jurisdiction/standing? How does de novo review differ from an appellate standard like abuse of discretion in similar contexts?

questions.title: Can a federal court compel OSC to follow § 1214 notice requirements during a § 1216 investigation?
questions.question_body: The opinion suggests that whether OSC must provide notices and information required by § 1214 in a § 1216 investigation is discretionary, citing *Carson v. U.S. Office of Special Counsel*. If so, does Congress allow courts to order OSC to adopt those procedural safeguards, or are they outside judicial control? Under what circumstances have courts imposed § 1214‑type procedures on investigations that are technically governed by § 1216?
